## Question

<!-- One sentence, naming the groups you compare. -->

Of each age group, what share has a hospital stay of 5 or more days, and does
this differ between women and men?

## Data

<!-- Where it's from, what one row is, how many rows. -->

- **Fairness:** Diabetes Hospital, 1999-2008. One row is one hospital
  encounter of a patient with diabetes. My file has
  `r scales::comma(nrow(fairness))` rows.
- **Sports:** Setka Cup table tennis. One row is one match. My file has
  `r scales::comma(nrow(sports))` rows.

## Older patients more often stay 5 days or more, in every race

## Quick change of scenery: In table tennis, the home player wins about half of all matches

```{r}
#| label: fig-b1
#| ref.label: b1
#| fig-alt: "Horizontal bars for matches of 3, 4 and 5 sets, each split into home wins and away wins, with about half of the matches won by the home player in every group."
```

## What it shows, and its limits

- The share of long stays differs by age group, and the pattern looks the
  same for all of the races. This describes a difference, not a cause.
- A stay of 5 or more days is my own cutoff, and the data cover US hospitals
  from 1999 to 2008, so they say nothing about today.
- In the Sports data, "home player" probably only means the first-listed
  player, so a 50% win rate is not evidence for a real home advantage.

**Sports:** Cassidy, G. (2024, July 17). Setka table tennis dataset – SCORE sports data repository. Scorenetwork.Org. https://data.scorenetwork.org/table_tennis/table_tennis_sept2022.html
